bearings.paper_claim: Crypto industry giving is projected north of 175 million dollars for 2025-2026, versus 145.5 million in 2023-2024, an off-year rise the report calls an outlier and attributes to the CLARITY Act push.
bearings.paper_location: Crypto section, line 9 of the text extract
bearings.system_side: Code applies one presidential factor u = 1.8635 to the general_giving measure on both cycle steps (UPLIFT_BOTH_STEPS at giving_forecast.py line 1425; gate at line 1888), so the 2025-26 midterm step is scaled by 1/1.8635, about minus 46 percent. Company PACs keep the fitted phi on the midterm step.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only applies if crypto giving is run through the general_giving measure, which was not checked. The report's 175 million is a projection with no stated method, window or source, so it is a counterexample to test, not evidence.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper line 9 confirmed, including the 175 million projection and the CLARITY attribution. Code description confirmed against the comment block and the gate. 1/1.8635 is about 0.537, so minus 46 percent is correct. The wrong-direction point holds only for the general_giving measure, so the bearing is restricted to that measure.

bearings.paper_claim: 2026 LDA reports show members Zach Nunn, Andy Kim, Young Kim, Bill Huizenga and others with an average increase of 20 interactions within the year, read as the community-bank industry pushing harder.
bearings.system_side: lobby_interactions.py reuses the build_network_2021_rebuild sponsor and cosponsor join for organization, bill and member attribution. The rebuild docstring (line 13) says each lobbied bill credits every legislator who sponsored or cosponsored it, so per-member counts from this join measure bill-roster overlap, not observed contact. The report never defines interactions or names its join.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies only if the report's interaction counts come from the bill-roster join, which the report does not say. If they come from described contacts, only the window and denominator flags remain.
bearings.verifier_note: Line 17 quote confirmed, including the four member names and the 20-interaction average, with no definition. The docstring confirms the sponsor and cosponsor credit rule. The analyst claim that LD-2 never names members is only partly backed here: lobby_interactions.py says filings name lobbyists and cite bills, not members. The refutation applies to reading the counts as contact evidence, not to the report's numbers, which cannot be checked from the extract.

bearings.paper_claim: Super PACs take 71.9 percent of crypto non-direct-to-candidate giving, which is 70 percent of industry giving; Fairshake is the 2nd largest super PAC and wholly crypto-funded; backed candidates won 38 of 40 primaries.
bearings.system_side: fec_build_beneficiary_tables seeds the traversal from each industry's funded committees (fec_beneficiary.R traversal_seed, around lines 1041-1060). Downstream rows carry a Support or Oppose direction (fec_beneficiary.R lines 136-145 and 348), so oppose money can be split from support money. An attributed-estimate view exists in the UI, but the route refuses with 409 until an estimate bundle exists (app/evidence-flow.js lines 8-10). A comment at R/export_guards.R line 278 says 89 percent of one shipped beneficiary sheet was opposition-direction rows.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 38 of 40 count has no window, no denominator of contested races and no baseline win rate. The 71.9 and 70 percent shares have no stated cycle or source. Reuse needs the support and oppose split by party and a stated cycle.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper lines 7, 9 and 13 confirmed as cited. The cited code range covers only seeding; the Support/Oppose partition and the 409 refusal sit in other lines, so the code_ref is narrowed. The 89 percent figure is a share of rows in one sheet, not of dollars as the analyst wrote. The paper's percentages and win counts cannot be reproduced from anything in the extract.

bearings.paper_claim: The C-suite share of crypto donations rose from 69 percent in 2021-22 to 98.8 percent in 2023-24; the report frames the credit union shortfall as missing employee and middle-management giving.
bearings.paper_location: Crypto section, line 7; abstract line 5 for the employee and middle-management framing
bearings.system_side: collect.R assigns Schedule A rows to roster companies by employer key (company_employer_keys, line 363). Occupation text enters only as an optional scoped regex on override rules (lines 520-529), keeping the most specific match. No C-suite or employee role taxonomy was found in that section.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An occupation-role split would need a hand-coded precision check. The report gives no coding rule for C-suite, so its 69 and 98.8 percent figures cannot be reproduced from the extract.
bearings.verifier_note: Line 7 and abstract line 5 confirmed. The code gap is confirmed: employer keys and an optional occupation regex, with no role split. The abstract does not use the word C-suite; that appears only at line 7, so the abstract citation is narrowed to the employee framing.

bearings.paper_claim: Crypto outspends key allies by factors of 100, so credit unions would have no chance in a monetary fight with the industry; the supporting graph is a missing placeholder.
bearings.system_side: The head-to-head pull uses a saturating term (x+1) over (x+1) plus HALFF times rcp, weighted by WM and added to a coalition term WP (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl lines 1096-1105). The dashboard prints the cannot fully offset message only when q is at least 1. The functional form is an assumption and is not validated against outcomes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The factor of 100 has no source, window or denominator, so the system cannot size the disadvantage. The bounded term shows only that the form caps the monetary pull, not that money decides outcomes.
bearings.verifier_note: Line 12 and placeholder line 11 confirmed. The formula and the q at least 1 branch match the description. The no-chance conclusion is not in the code; the code bounds the monetary term and computes a break-even spend. The bounded pull description is accurate as a statement about the functional form only.

related.why: A 2025 work on the crypto lobby in American politics; the report's Crypto section could be checked against it. Not checked against the text here.

Furnas, LaPira and Brock find low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which bears on the report's implicit reading of LDA activity and giving as one push. The report does not state that reading, so this is not a direct contradiction. Relation changed from contradicts to complements.
Randomized field experiment on contributions and access; the nearest tested version of the report's money-buys-attention claim, which the report leaves untested. Use access wording, not influence.
LobbyView bill-level LDA data is the likely source of the bill-roster join behind the per-member counts. The report does not name its source, so this link is inferred.
Work on dynamics of the US lobbying network, relevant to the cycle-phase assumption. Its cycle-synchronization claim was not checked against the Bacik text here.
Tests the sequencing of donations and lobbying, the assumption behind combining FEC and LDA evidence in the report. The report does not test sequencing itself.

summary_issues: The rounding explanation for the 8,162.6 percent versus about 8,167 percent gap holds: an unrounded base near 1.7609, displayed as 1.76, gives 8,162.6 percent. The report should state the unrounded base.
The summary reads the community-bank 20-interaction figure as lobbying-contact evidence. The report never defines interactions, so the figure should be labeled undefined rather than refuted.
The summary says the per-member LDA counts use LDA as a weight source that D-021 bars. That is an inference from the bill-roster join, not a statement in the report, and should be marked inferred.
The summary places the C-suite framing in the abstract. Abstract line 5 names employee and middle-management giving; C-suite appears only at line 7.

The transfer-graph code_ref is narrowed: fec_beneficiary.R lines 1041-1060 cover seeding only. The Support/Oppose partition is at lines 136-145 and 348. The 89 percent figure counts rows in one sheet (R/export_guards.R line 278), not dollars.
The summary implies the midterm factor applies to crypto-like industries. The code applies it only to the general_giving measure; the measure assignment for crypto was not checked.
The summary states that Fairshake is the 2nd largest super PAC and wholly crypto-funded. Those are the report's claims at line 9, with no date or metric, not verified facts.

The summary omits that the abstract promises five industries but the extract contains only Crypto and Community Banks. Credit Union, Financial Technologies and Credit Arms sections are absent from this file.
The summary's descriptions of a self-destructive feedback loop and money buying attention are author judgments with no test, not findings.
The 4.3 million credit union target and its implied baseline of about 3.05 million are derived by the analyst and do not appear in the text. Flag as derived, not reported.
The extract has no Paul markup (no highlights or notes), so Paul-note items are none; coverage is the full 21-line extract.
